blocks.text: Hence the diminutive trulla [ladle]. Varro, De lingua Latina, book 4: Trulla from its likeness to the trua; because that is large and this small, as it were truula. Nonius: The ancients wished the trua to be named from terere [to rub], which we call by the diminutive trulla. Hence, then, truo is the onocrotalus. Festus: Truo, the bird onocrotalus. Caecilius, mocking the size of a nose: "O immortal gods, whence has this truo crept forth?" The Glosses of Philoxenus: Ὀνοκρόταλος [Onokrotalos], Trica; read Truo. Other Glosses, excellent but often corrupted by the carelessness of copyists, have Triduo, tinuero. One should read Trua [is] a vessel; Truo, however, ὀνοκρόταλον [onokrotalon]; supply sonat [means]. The bird is evidently called truo from the trua [ladle] that it has in its beak. Accordingly the Savoyards call it gutturosa, that is, strumosa [the goitred one], from the crop which protrudes from the throat like a goitre. And most of the Arabs call it الحوصل [al-ḥawṣal] alhausal, that is, the crop, as if the whole bird were a crop. Thus the Indian bird κήλας [kēlas] in Aelian, book 16, ch. 4, three times larger than the bustard, with a huge mouth and great legs, having πρηγορεῶνα, καὶ ἐκεῖνον μέγιστον, προσεμφερῆ κωρύκῳ [prēgoreōna, kai ekeinon megiston, prosempherē kōrykō], a crop, and that a very large one, like a sack, is certainly the onocrotalus, which the Greeks would have called κήλας [kēlas] on account of its κήλη [kēlē], or βρογχοκήλη [bronchokēlē], that is, a swelling in the throat. Nor is that crop said without reason to be very large, since some write that it holds almost an amphora or an urn. Others report that a little Ethiopian child was found in it. Others relate that they put into it a fist together with the arm, others a foot [III, 18] with the leg up to the knee, the animal itself remaining unharmed. Others that they put it on their head as a hood, the rest of the body hanging down behind. Others that Egyptian sailors bail out the bilge with the beak of the onocrotalus. And Pliny (book 10, chapter 47) says that in the throat itself there is a kind of second stomach. Into this the insatiable animal heaps everything, so that its capacity is astonishing. Then, when its plundering is complete, it gradually returns the food from there into the mouth and passes it into the true (others read the lower) belly, in the manner of a ruminant. Hence it is that an Arab poet, ملغز [mulghiz], that is, αἰνιγματιζόμενος [ainigmatizomenos] [speaking in riddles], says of this bird,
ما طاير في قلبه * يلوح للناس عجب * منقاره كبطنه * والعين منه في الذنب * [mā ṭāyir fī qalbihi * yalūḥu li-l-nās ʿajab * minqāruhu ka-baṭnihi * wa-l-ʿayn minhu fī al-dhanab *]
